entry.evidence: there is also a large diversity on the earthquake generation models

steps.action: Pose the question of how to evaluate the earthquake generation (recurrence) models used in PSHA for slowly deforming regions, applied to W and SW Iberia.
steps.quote: propose a methodology to evaluate and validate earthquake generation models that are used for PSHA studies

steps.action: Fix the premise of the test: elastic rebound, with earthquakes in the study area driven only by tectonic strain, so that the strain rate is a scale against which the models are compared. Gravitational potential energy and GIA contributions are set aside, citing Neres et al. 2018 and Bird and Kagan 2004.
steps.quote: earthquakes are generated only by tectonic stresses controlled by the horizontal strain rate

steps.action: Assemble the rival recurrence models from five published PSHA studies (EC8, ERSTA, SHARE min/med/max, QREN, VF2007 with 32 logic-tree branches) for two source zones, the Lower Tagus Valley and the 1755 offshore zone (Tables 1-4).
steps.quote: For this investigation we consider five different PSHA studies

steps.action: Design two consistency tests: a simple rule-of-thumb slip-rate test and a complex test based on dynamic neotectonic modelling. Dynamic modelling is chosen over kinematic modelling because kinematic modelling cannot estimate offshore deformation consistently.
steps.quote: we propose two tests on the earthquake recurrence models used to make PSHA studies, one simple, rule-of-thumb type and the other based on numerical modelling

steps.action: Convert the cumulative seismic moment rate implied by each model's DTGR law into a slip rate on a single representative fault, with c=1 and the L, H, mu values of Table 5 (results in Tables 8-9).
steps.quote: the seismic strain is converted into a relative velocity between blocks

steps.action: Expand the VF2007 discrete logic-tree distribution into a continuous slip-rate distribution by Monte Carlo sampling of a and b. Select five representative scenarios from 20% probability classes for the complex test (Figs. 6-7).
steps.quote: We will expand the resulting discrete probability distribution into a continuous probability distribution through a Monte Carlo simulation

steps.action: Take the long-term lithospheric deformation of the Africa-Iberia plate boundary from the SHELLS finite-element neotectonic model of Neres et al. (2016), co-authored by members of this team.
steps.quote: That work was performed for the Africa–Eurasia plate boundary extending from the Gloria Fault to the northern Algerian margin by Neres et al. (2016).

steps.action: Modify the long-term seismicity code (Bird and Liu 2007; Bird et al. 2010) to use source zones instead of plate boundaries and to take the PSHA recurrence parameters, translated from DTGR to TGR by a non-linear fit.
steps.quote: Firstly, we introduced the parametrization of zones, instead of plate boundaries.

steps.action: Check the DTGR-to-TGR translation by comparing the total seismic moment release of the original and fitted laws (Supplement S3).
steps.quote: The quality of the fit was assessed by comparing the total seismic moment release computed for both models, DTGR and fitted TGR.

steps.action: Compile the kinematic knowledge used as reference: plate convergence of about 4 mm/yr, GNSS intraplate deformation below 1 mm/yr, and geological and neotectonic fault slip rates below 0.1-0.5 mm/yr.
steps.quote: Once this rotation is removed, the intraplate deformation is less than 1 mm yr - 1 everywhere (ibid.).

steps.action: Set the acceptance bounds for the simple test: upper limits of 1 mm/yr (LTV) and 4 mm/yr (1755 zone); lower suspect limits of 0.1 and 0.5 mm/yr.
steps.quote: we assume 1 mm yr - 1 as a reasonable kinematic reference value for the simple sanity check

steps.action: Compute long-term seismicity (LTS) rates per magnitude class and moment rates from the neotectonic deformation, and form TGR/LTS ratios for each model (Tables 10-11). Ratios near or above 1, or below 0.1, are taken as suspect.
steps.quote: It is expressed by the ratio of PSHA recurrence model parameters over the long-term seismicity estimate.

steps.action: Compare all 11 models per zone against both tests' criteria in a summary table (Table 12).
steps.quote: We present in Table 12 a summary of the sanity tests (simple and complex) performed on the 11 PSHA earthquake generation models

steps.action: For the LTV zone, flag EC8, ERSTA, SHAREmin and SHAREmax as excessive, SHAREmed as suspect, and QREN as too low. The five VF2007 scenarios pass.
steps.quote: clearly identifies three models with excessive earthquake generation

steps.action: For the 1755 zone, flag EC8 and ERSTA as excessive, SHAREmax as suspect, and QREN and four of five VF2007 scenarios as too low. Only SHAREmin, SHAREmed and one VF2007 scenario pass.
steps.quote: The complex consistency test identifies scenarios EC8 and ERSTA as being clearly excessive in earthquake generation

steps.action: Cross-check the simple test against the complex test: the two agree on 20 of 22 model classifications.
steps.quote: the simplified consistency check evaluation agrees with the more elaborate one on 20 out of the 22 PSHA earthquake generation models

steps.action: Compare the full Monte Carlo VF2007 distribution with the simple-test bounds: 10% exceed the bound in LTV, and 40% fall below it in the 1755 zone.
steps.quote: for the 1755 source zone, 40 % of the investigated models should be considered suspect for generating too few earthquakes

steps.action: Check that the two complex-test indicators, the activity ratio by magnitude class and the moment-rate ratio, give the same classification.
steps.quote: The results obtained show that both indicators result in the same classification of the PSHA models.

steps.action: Keep the claim that both tests can screen PSHA recurrence models in slowly deforming regions, and recommend that they enter PSHA weighting schemes.
steps.quote: Both tests can be used to assess the consistency of PSHA models.

end.claim: Two consistency tests (a simple slip-rate test and a complex test using neotectonic long-term seismicity) can screen PSHA recurrence models in slowly deforming regions; they agree on 20 of 22 models and flag several published SW Iberia models as excessive or deficient in moment release.

decisive_move.sentence: Modifying the long-term seismicity code to take source zones and the PSHA recurrence parameters lets the complex test turn neotectonic deformation into rates comparable with each PSHA model; without it the complex test could not be run.

gates.evidence: No new data were acquired; all inputs are published (Data availability). The models could fail the moment-budget tests and several did, and the two tests could have disagreed. The thresholds (1/4 mm/yr upper, 0.1/0.5 mm/yr lower, ratio near or above 1 or below 0.1) are stated in §5.1 ¶8 and §5.2 ¶1, with no indication that they were fixed before the results were computed.

imports.item: Klemeš's critique of statistical extreme-flood forecasting from short records, used as an analogy
Monte Carlo propagation of uncertainty in the Gutenberg-Richter a and b parameters
Finite-element solution of the stress equilibrium equation (SHELLS code)

novelty_claims.quote: We propose two consistency tests to address the variability of earthquake generation models found in PSHA studies
propose a methodology to evaluate and validate earthquake generation models that are used for PSHA studies

limits: No review file or discussion was supplied, although the paper went through NHESS open discussion (referees Geller and Cabieces are named), so no review sequence is coded. The abstract says the analysis allowed a downgrade of model weights, but no reweighted hazard is computed or shown. The thresholds for 'suspect' were chosen by the authors after compiling the reference data; nothing shows they were fixed in advance, and 'close to 1' is applied loosely (SHAREmin at 1.046 is called excessive in LTV, SHAREmax at 0.991 suspect in the 1755 zone). The sensitivity to L, H, mu and coupling is argued analytically (linear scaling) and deferred to the reader, not computed (§4.1 ¶8, §5.3 ¶5). The text has inconsistencies: 'three models' with four listed (§5.3 ¶1), and 'VF2002' (§5.3 ¶2). The neotectonic model is inherited from co-authors (Neres et al. 2016), and QREN is the co-authors' own earlier model. The 'observations' the LTS rates are compared with are themselves model outputs (inference). Sub-claims and their status: the classification of individual published models as excessive or deficient is best_explanation under the stated auxiliaries (tectonic-only strain, perfect coupling, chosen geometry). The explanation of poor performance in the 1755 zone by poor geological control is untested (inference). Composition is none_fits: a method proposal applied to many published rival models through a shared screening test, without exclusions refined into survivors (not strong inference) and without a phenomenon to establish (not capability_first).

disagreements.support: Argues that decisions on building codes must still be made and that PSHA can be improved by physical constraints; no new evidence is offered.
disagreements.quote: We do not follow Mulargia et al.'s (2017) proposal to completely abandon PSHA

disagreements.target: Common attribution of PSHA result diversity mainly to GMPEs
disagreements.support: Shows a large spread in implied moment release among the recurrence models themselves.
disagreements.quote: which cannot be ascribed only to the choice of the ground motion prediction equations

disagreements.target: Published EC8, ERSTA and SHARE recurrence models (Campos Costa et al. 2008; Carrilho et al. 2010; Woessner et al. 2015)
disagreements.support: Their implied slip rates and TGR/LTS ratios exceed the geodetic and neotectonic moment budget (Tables 8, 10-12).
disagreements.quote: clearly identifies three models with excessive earthquake generation

disagreements.target: QREN recurrence model (Matias and Teves-Costa 2011a, b) and most VF2007 scenarios for the 1755 zone
disagreements.support: Implied moment release is far below the tectonic budget (ratios below about 0.13; slip rate 0.06 mm/yr in LTV).
disagreements.quote: The QREN model shows too little earthquake generation, confirmed by both sanity checks, simple and complex.

disagreements.target: Mixed fault-zone source model of Rivas-Medina et al. (2018)
disagreements.support: Argues that fault activity in W and SW Iberia is too poorly known for the approach.
disagreements.quote: This is an exceptional case that cannot be extended to the whole W and SW Iberia.

disagreements.target: Kinematic deformation modelling (Bird 2009; Carafa et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: Argues that offshore results are controlled by the subjective choice of faults and leave no independent data for testing.
disagreements.quote: However, it does not allow consistent estimation of the offshore long-term deformation
